title: break, next, and redo
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of break, next, and redo in a Ruby program and name the key rule involved.
Apply break, next, and redo in a small example and predict its result before running it.
Identify one boundary or failure case related to control flow inside nested structures and verify the intended behavior.

content.intro: Learn break, next, and redo through a visual model, a minimal Ruby example, and a practical check.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding break, next, and redo helps you write code that is easier to explain, test, and maintain. It also helps separate Ruby language guarantees from runtime assumptions, dependency behavior, and application-specific rules.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: break, next, and redo helps you reason about exiting a loop. In Ruby, prefer a small example whose inputs and expected result are easy to explain. This lesson connects the syllabus topic to practical code and highlights where assumptions or edge cases matter.

content_blocks.title: How to think about it
content_blocks.text: Begin by identifying the key rule: Exiting a loop. Then connect it to Skipping an iteration. The remaining syllabus points—Repeating an iteration, Control flow inside nested structures—are useful checks before applying this in a larger project.

content_blocks.title: Example: break, next, and redo
content_blocks.code:
(1..5).each do |number|
  next if number.even?
  puts number
end

items.text: Test an empty value, a boundary value, and one invalid value before depending on the behavior.

items.title: Treating an example as a universal rule

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Run the example as written, compare it with the expected result, and explain why each line supports break, next, and redo. Next change one input or condition and predict the result before running it.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a second example for break, next, and redo using a different input. Add one edge case from the syllabus list (Control flow inside nested structures), state the expected behavior, and write a small test or manual check that would catch a regression.

content_blocks.title: Run, troubleshoot, and reset
content_blocks.text: Save as lesson.rb and run `ruby lesson.rb` from a terminal. CodeLeaf currently has no isolated Ruby runner, so these examples should be run locally until one is deployed. If the command fails, confirm `ruby --version`, inspect the full error message, and verify that required standard-library or gem dependencies are installed. Reset by removing temporary files created by your experiment and returning the code to the smallest reproducible example.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain break, next, and redo, identify its place in conditional logic and control flow, run a focused example, and verify an important boundary. Revisit the linked exercise if this is a core topic; advanced runtime or framework examples remain draft until reviewed in a suitable environment.
